subject: money
topic: Forgetting to cancel is a business model
angle: While consumer inattention and switching costs can double seller revenues, complex bundling of services can actually decrease customer retention during onboarding.
title: The Profit of Inattention

hooks.text: Why do you keep paying for things you don't use?
You think you are forgetting. They are counting on it.
You are paying a tax on your own inattention.
A cursor hovering over a tiny grey button.
Forgetting to cancel is a business model.

reveal.headline: Inattention doubles seller revenues.
reveal.body: Cancellation frictions driven by inattention or switching costs roughly double seller revenues on average. This finding is based on stylized models rather than a direct experimental trial.

explain.headline: Complexity creates friction.
explain.body: Adding more services can decrease customer retention during onboarding. This is likely because the perceived complexity of the bundle deters people from staying.

matters.headline: The architecture of choice.
matters.body: That may be why systems are designed to be difficult to leave. Profit relies on your willingness to overlook the effort of clicking away.

example.headline: The monthly bill.
example.body: You sit at your kitchen table. You see a charge on your bank app for a service you haven't used in months. You decide it is too much effort to find the cancel button tonight.

question.headline: How much of your money is spent on things you intend to stop using?

stat.label: the effect of cancellation frictions driven by inattention

claims.text: Cancellation frictions driven by inattention or switching costs roughly double seller revenues on average, holding fixed initial subscribers.
claims.quote: Using two stylized models of consumer inertia—driven by inattention or switching costs—we estimate that these cancellation frictions roughly double seller revenues on average, holding fixed initial subscribers.

claims.text: Bundling more add-on services can significantly decrease customer retention during the onboarding stage.
claims.quote: A field study involving a B2B SaaS provider further reveals that bundling more add-on services can significantly decrease customer retention during the onboarding stage.

claims.text: Months during which cards are replaced, when active renewal is required, are associated with much higher rates of cancellation.
claims.quote: We use comprehensive data from a large payment card network to document that months during which cards are replaced, when active renewal is required, are associated with much higher rates of cancellation.

claims.text: Complexity perceptions are the likely source of the detrimental effects of add-on bundling during the customer onboarding stage.
claims.quote: Finally, a cross-industry survey of B2B managers identifies complexity perceptions as the likely source of these detrimental effects of add-on bundling during the customer onboarding stage.

claims.text: The effectiveness of digital goods subscriptions remains controversial in terms of the profitability for different supply chain members, including content providers and retailers.
claims.quote: However, the effectiveness of digital goods subscriptions remains controversial in terms of the profitability for different supply chain members, including content providers and retailers.

verdict: The evidence shows that while inattention creates significant profit for sellers, other factors like service complexity can negatively impact customer retention.
caveat: One study showing the link between inattention and revenue is based on stylized models rather than a direct experimental trial.
caption:
Forgetting to cancel is a deliberate design choice.

Research shows that inattention and switching costs roughly double seller revenues, though this is based on stylized models. Simultaneously, complex service bundles can actually hurt retention during onboarding.

What is the most difficult subscription for you to cancel?
